meta.rounding: Every dollar figure below is shown rounded to the nearest $10, per the project instruction. Unrounded values are used inside the model and rounded only for display.
meta.verified_vs_assumption: Entries with status verified_official carry a source_id into sources.json. Entries with status model_assumption are planning inputs with no official parcel-level source; each states its basis and range.

assumptions.name: Long-run home price appreciation, base case
assumptions.basis: Anchored to the FHFA all-transactions California HPI: the index went from 424.32 (2004Q1) to 974.97 (2026Q2), a 21.6-year compound rate of about 3.9%. A 3% base case sits below that to reflect a below-trend period and the Census estimate that Cupertino's population fell 3.2% between 2020 and 2025.

assumptions.name: Long-run home price appreciation, Property B
assumptions.basis: Same statewide anchor; San Francisco has underperformed the state recently, so the low end of the range is the more conservative read.

assumptions.name: General inflation (cost escalation)
assumptions.basis: The 2026-27 California CPI change used by the BOE was 3.307%, and the 2% Prop 13 assessment cap binds separately. 2.5% is used for non-property-tax operating costs so they stay above the 2% assessment cap but below the recent CPI spike.

assumptions.name: Annual property tax assessment growth cap
assumptions.basis: Article XIII A §2(b); BOE set the 2026-27 factor at 1.02.

assumptions.name: Property tax composite rate, Property A (Cupertino)
assumptions.basis: Deliberately uses the rate IMPLIED by the user's own 2025 figures ($7,210 / $539,740 = 1.3358%) rather than the county's illustrative 1.1488%, because the implied rate reproduces the actual bills and the illustrative rate does not. A lower-bound sensitivity uses the county's 1.1488% typical TRA.

assumptions.name: Property tax composite rate, Property B (San Francisco)
assumptions.basis: Uses the rate implied by the user's 2025 figures ($2,440 / $114,250 = 2.136%) for the same reason as Property A. Note this is 81% above SF's published 1.18162182% secured rate, which is the largest single irregularity in the supplied data and is flagged.

assumptions.name: Post-1979 San Francisco building coverage
assumptions.basis: Whether Property B falls under the SF Rent Ordinance (pre-6/13/1979 building) or only AB 1482 cannot be determined without the property's age, which is not supplied. The model runs AB 1482's SF-area CPI test as the more conservative of the two for the 2026–27 window and flags the uncertainty.

assumptions.name: Rent growth, base case
assumptions.basis: Both properties are rent-regulated. SF's current allowable increase is 1.6% and AB 1482's current window is 8.8% for the SF CPI area, but AB 1482 also sunsets on 1/1/2030. A flat 2% is used across the whole horizon as a neutral planning number between the two regimes and is flagged as an assumption, not a legal entitlement.

assumptions.name: Home insurance, Property A
assumptions.basis: User estimate. No official parcel-level premium is published for either ZIP. Escalated at general inflation thereafter. The sensitivity uses $3,000/yr, the top of the plausible Bay Area range for a high-value dwelling with earthquake coverage added separately.

assumptions.name: Landlord insurance, Property B
assumptions.basis: User estimate. A three-unit rented building in the Outer Sunset at $1,500/yr is low relative to typical Bay Area premiums for that exposure; the sensitivity doubles it.

assumptions.name: Earthquake insurance
assumptions.basis: Not included in any figure because no coverage amount was supplied and no official parcel-level premium exists. Flagged explicitly: standard California HO-3 policies exclude earthquake, and the California Earthquake Authority is the usual market. This is a real, unmodelled cost.

assumptions.name: Maintenance and repair reserve, Property A
assumptions.units: fraction of market value per year
assumptions.basis: A 0.75%/yr reserve on a $3.1M home is about $23,000/yr, consistent with the user's note that Property A needs less upkeep than Property B. Escalated at general inflation rather than at home-price appreciation so the reserve does not balloon on paper.

assumptions.name: Maintenance and repair reserve, Property B
assumptions.units: fraction of market value per year
assumptions.basis: Higher than Property A per the user's own comparison; a Century-old three-unit wood-frame building in the Outer Sunset carries roof, foundation, sewer-lateral and seismic-refit exposure.

assumptions.name: Vacancy and credit loss
assumptions.basis: Standard planning allowance for a small rent-controlled building; the two current tenancies are long-standing, so the true recent number is closer to zero, but a 4% allowance is used for prudence.

assumptions.name: Water and sewer, Property A
assumptions.basis: Midpoint of the user's $100–$150 range. Cross-checked against San Jose Water's Schedule 1: an $79.67 monthly service charge plus roughly 10 ccf at $5.04–$7.52/ccf lands near $135–$155 for water alone before sewer, so the user's range is plausible and possibly at the low end if the parcel is on an SJW meter. Escalated at general inflation.

assumptions.name: Water and sewer, Property B (all three units)
assumptions.basis: Midpoint of the user's $330–$400 range. Cross-checked against SFPUC Schedule W-1B and Schedule A: a 5/8-inch service charge of $19.65, tier-1 volume at $12.03 per ccf per dwelling unit, wastewater volume at $20.74 per discharge unit at a 95% flow factor, and Tier 3 stormwater of $29.55/mo. Thirteen ccf/month across three units reproduces roughly $330–$380 all-in, so the user's range is consistent with published tariffs.

assumptions.name: Net electricity, Property A (after solar)
assumptions.basis: User reports no bill and roughly $10–$20/month of net credit. Modelled as a $15/month credit. Important caveat: the CPUC closed the NEM tariffs to new enrollments and moved new interconnections to the Net Billing Tariff from 4/15/2023 at avoided-cost export values. Whether the existing system keeps retail-rate credits depends on its original interconnection date, which is not supplied. Both cases are modelled.

assumptions.name: Electricity, Property B
assumptions.basis: Midpoint of the user's $30–$70 range for the whole building. Low because tenants carry their own accounts in most Outer Sunset configurations; confirm which accounts are on the owner.

assumptions.name: Property management and leasing
assumptions.basis: Standard 5–8% for small residential in the Bay Area. Only applied in the rent-out scenario for Property A, and to Property B if the owner no longer lives on site.

assumptions.name: Reinvestment return, reinvestment scenario
assumptions.units: fraction per year, nominal, before tax
assumptions.basis: A 60/40-style balanced portfolio planning number. Cross-checked to the Treasury curve on 2026-11-09: 10-year par yield 4.88%, 20-year 5.29%, 30-year 5.26%, so a risk-free-only alternative is materially lower and equity exposure is what supports 6.5%. Tax drag is modelled separately, never folded into this number.

assumptions.name: Portfolio income yield (dividends/interest actually received)
assumptions.basis: Separates the part of the return that produces taxable cash flow from the part that is unrealized appreciation, which matters because the reinvestment path is taxed on realized income and gains only.

assumptions.name: Effective tax rate on portfolio income
assumptions.basis: Combines federal 15%–20% long-term rates (plus 3.8% NIIT where applicable) with California taxing the same gains as ordinary income under its own brackets. 33% is a blended planning rate, not a marginal rate for any one year.

assumptions.name: Effective tax rate on net rental income
assumptions.basis: Rental income is ordinary income for both federal and California purposes. 37% blends federal 24%–32% with California 9.3%–10.3%. Note that §121 does not shelter rental income and that depreciation recapture at 25% applies to any residential depreciation actually claimed.

assumptions.name: Residential rental depreciation
assumptions.basis: IRS Publication 527 describes residential rental property depreciation over 27.5 years. Depreciable basis excludes land; the land share of a Bay Area parcel is high, so the shelter is smaller than a simple 1/27.5 of value.

assumptions.name: Land share of value, Property A
assumptions.basis: Single-family Bay Area parcels commonly carry 50–70% of value in land; land is not depreciable.

assumptions.name: Cost of sale (commission, escrow, title, transfer tax)
assumptions.basis: Composed of a 5% brokerage commission plus roughly 0.11% Santa Clara County transfer tax for Property A (0.75% SF transfer tax for Property B) plus escrow, title and recording. SF's transfer tax is a whole-value bracket so it is applied from the published tier table, not from this blended number.

assumptions.name: Year of inheritance
assumptions.basis: Midpoint of the stated 2040–2050 window. The model also reports 2040 and 2050 so the sensitivity is visible rather than buried.

assumptions.name: Probate avoidance through a funded trust
assumptions.basis: A funded revocable trust is the usual California tool for avoiding probate on real property. If the properties are actually titled in the trust, the transfer to the heirs is by trust administration and trustee deed rather than probate. Probate fees are statutory in California and can be large on a multi-million-dollar estate, so confirming trust funding is one of the highest-value checks available. Exact fee amounts are NOT modelled here because they depend on the statutory schedule applying to the estate and cannot be confirmed without the estate's facts.

scenario_inputs.name: Live in Property A
scenario_inputs.description: Heir moves in, claims the Prop 19 parent-child exclusion plus the homeowners' exemption, keeps Property B and its rent, and holds Property A long term.

scenario_inputs.name: Rent out Property A
scenario_inputs.description: Heir does not occupy Property A. Prop 19 does not apply, so Property A is reassessed at market value on inheritance. Heir stays in Property B and collects rent from both properties.
scenario_inputs.rent_a_basis: No official rent for this specific home; a $5,400/month single-family planning rent is used and escalated at 2%/yr. The sensitivity runs $4,500–$7,000.

scenario_inputs.name: Sell Property A and reinvest
scenario_inputs.description: Heir sells shortly after inheritance, pays cost of sale and any capital-gains tax on the excess over the stepped-up basis, and invests the proceeds. Property B is retained and stays rented.
